---
title: "7. Marker genes and biological annotation"
---

## From cluster IDs to biology

After clustering you have labels such as 0, 1, 2, 3. Marker testing asks which genes are enriched in a cluster relative to a comparison set.

```r
markers <- FindAllMarkers(obj, only.pos = TRUE)
head(markers)
```

A marker is not necessarily uniquely expressed. It is often a gene with a systematic difference in expression level and/or prevalence.

## Multi-gene annotation

Prefer coherent programs over single markers.

- T cells: `CD3D`, `CD3E`, `TRAC`
- B cells: `MS4A1`, `CD79A`, `CD74`
- NK cells: `NKG7`, `GNLY`, `KLRD1`, `PRF1` with weak/absent T-cell receptor genes
- Myeloid: `LST1`, `TYROBP`, `FCER1G`, `CTSS`

A cluster with high NKG7 is not automatically NK because cytotoxic CD8 T cells can also express NKG7.

## Cell type versus cell state

A useful hierarchy is:

- **type/lineage:** T cell, B cell, NK, monocyte
- **state:** naive-like, cytotoxic, IFN-stimulated, proliferating, exhaustion-associated

Do not force every transcriptional state into a new "cell type."

## Statistical significance versus biological significance

With thousands of cells, extremely small expression differences can generate tiny p-values. Evaluate effect size, fraction expressing, replicate consistency, and pathway/program coherence.

::: {.callout-warning}
Cluster-marker p-values do not solve pseudoreplication for condition-level biological inference. Cluster description and patient-level differential expression are different statistical questions.
:::
